system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 9 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2125-08-04 14:38:00 to 2125-08-12 14:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with advanced HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, tracheostomy and PEG dependence, and a history of osteonecrosis was readmitted for tachypnea and coffee-ground emesis. He had recently been discharged after treatment for pseudomonal UTI. Evaluation revealed leukocytosis and elevated lactate, with concern for aspiration pneumonitis due to inappropriate oral intake at rehab. Chest imaging showed chronic interstitial lung disease without new consolidation. He improved with supportive care, including suctioning and nebulizers, and did not require antibiotic escalation despite Pseudomonas growth in sputum. A brief SVT episode resolved with vagal maneuvers. Trazodone was discontinued after contributing to altered mental status. Pain from chronic osteonecrosis was managed with acetaminophen. He stabilized, completed treatment, and was discharged back to rehabilitation with updated orders for NPO status and medication adjustments.
problems: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food or vomitus
Other dependence on machines, supplemental oxygen
Aseptic necrosis of head and neck of femur
Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Chronic airway obstruction, not elsewhere classified
Pseudomonas infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site
Chronic ulcer of other specified sites
Antidepressants causing adverse effects in therapeutic use

ANESTHESIA: Sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of 0 mcg of
fentanyl and 2 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service time of 23
minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously
monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine was injected
in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.

PROCEDURE:  1. Replacement of a ___ low profile 3.5 cm stomal length MIC
gastrojejunostomy tube.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
supine on the exam table.  A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The tube site was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.
A scout image of the abdomen was obtained.  This showed that the existing
gastrojejunostomy tube was partially coiled in the stomach.  A stiff glide
wire was advanced through the existing tube, but this exacerbated the loop in
the stomach.  Therefore, a Glidewire was advanced over a Kumpe catheter
alongside the existing tube through the same hole into the stomach.  The wire
was removed a contrast injection was performed to confirm positioning within
the stomach.  Over a 6 ___ sheath, the Glidewire and Kumpe catheter were
directed into the jejunum.  The wire was removed and a contrast injection was
performed to confirm positioning.  Then the Glidewire was exchanged for a
stiff Glidewire over the Kumpe catheter.  The Kumpe catheter and sheath were
then removed.  A new 18 ___ MIC gastrojejunostomy tube was then advanced
over the stiff Glidewire, after removing the existing gastrojejunostomy tube. 
The balloon was inflated.  A contrast injection was performed to confirm
positioning.  The tube was then flushed.
The patient tolerated the procedure well and there were no immediate
complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You were brought in because of a fever. Do you remember that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Felt warm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. Your white blood cell count was high, which means your body is fighting something. We think it’s a urinary tract infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I’ve had those before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and this one is caused by a tough bacteria called Pseudomonas. It’s resistant to many antibiotics, so we’re using one called cefepime through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we caught it early. You’re not showing signs of serious illness, and your lungs and heart look stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel okay now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your urine culture. It grew Pseudomonas and another bacteria, but the team thinks only Pseudomonas needs treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why not both?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because the other one might just be contamination. You’re improving, so we don’t need to treat everything that grows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back clean—no bacteria in the blood. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So infection is only in urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And your breathing is stable. We’ll keep supporting your oxygen through the trach and continue the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an X-ray of your right hip today because you pointed to it as painful. No new fracture. The osteonecrosis is still there, same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hurts more sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep giving acetaminophen for that. It’s the safest option with your other conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re halfway through your antibiotic course. Fever is gone, white count is coming down. That’s progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a CT scan tomorrow to see why you keep getting UTIs. Could be a stone or something structural.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Like a kidney stone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It might explain the repeat infections. We’ll check that and see if a urologist needs to get involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your GJ tube was successfully exchanged today. It was due, and the old one had shifted into the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was that a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could have caused blockage or poor feeding. The new one is placed correctly in the jejunum. You can keep getting your feeds as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. You have a 6 mm stone in the right ureter, near the bladder. It’s not blocking anything now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it need to come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not urgently. But it might be why you keep getting infections. We’re referring you to urology for follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I drink more water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that helps. But with your feeding tube, we’ll make sure your fluids are adjusted properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve now completed your 7-day IV antibiotic course. Your labs look much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m done with IV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. No oral antibiotics needed. The infection is cleared. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re ready to go back to your facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. When?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Probably day after tomorrow. We’ll make sure everything is set for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re finalizing your discharge plan. You’ll go back to your care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I see urology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve referred you. They’ll check if the stone needs treatment to prevent more infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my HIV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue exactly as before—Darunavir, ritonavir, Truvada. And your prophylaxis for infections: atovaquone and azithromycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Seizure meds too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Keppra twice a day. And citalopram for mood, Ativan if anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Acetaminophen for hip pain. No NSAIDs—they’re not safe with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also saw your bladder wall is thickened, which suggests chronic irritation. That’s another reason to follow up with urology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: From the stone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Or from long-term catheter use. They’ll evaluate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just—am I safe going back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Infection is treated, pain is managed, and your feeding tube is working. Just keep up with your fluids and follow up with urology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sister will be contacted before discharge. She’s listed as your contact.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your trach care and oxygen will continue as before. The facility has the orders.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also send a note to your infectious disease clinic. They’ll want to know about the resistant Pseudomonas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’ve seen that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and they’ll help monitor for recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your hip pain. Keep using acetaminophen. If it worsens, let your team know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And no changes to your feeding—continue tube feeds at goal rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The transport team will get you ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Stay hydrated and keep up with your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your facility gets all the updates.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And if you develop fever or pain again, they’ll know to check your urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Have a safe trip back.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with advanced HIV/AIDS, chronic respiratory failure, tracheostomy and GJ tube dependence, and a history of osteonecrosis was admitted for fever. Evaluation revealed leukocytosis and a urinary tract infection caused by resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa. He was treated with a 7-day course of IV cefepime, with improvement in symptoms and labs. A CT scan identified a 6 mm stone in the right ureter, which may contribute to recurrent infections, prompting a urology referral. His GJ tube was exchanged during admission due to malposition. Chronic conditions, including HIV, seizures, and right hip pain from osteonecrosis, were managed with ongoing medications. He remained stable, completed treatment, and was discharged back to his extended care facility with follow-up plans.
